report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Risks and Opportunities in Digital Media Interventions for Youth: A Scientometric Review

text.text: Youth must navigate both the opportunities and risks associated with digital media.
This scientometric review examined 120 empirical studies on digital media interventions for youth and used the 4C framework (content, contact, conduct, and contract) to map their thematic focus.
Scientometric mapping techniques were applied to explore keyword co-occurrence patterns and collaboration networks.
Most interventions addressed either risks or opportunities separately (58.3%), whereas 39.2% combined risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension.
Only 2.5% integrated multiple 4C dimensions.
Interventions predominantly focused on content and conduct, with limited attention to contact and contract, including topics like social interactions, privacy, digital rights, and commercialization.
Collaboration patterns were fragmented, with researchers working within thematic clusters rather than across them, despite drawing on a shared conceptual foundation.
These findings suggest that current interventions cover only part of the 4C framework.
Future research should encourage more integrated, cross-dimensional interventions and stronger collaboration among researchers.
In an era where digital media is increasingly integral to everyday life, young people are at the forefront of both the promises and the perils of rapidly evolving technology (Livingstone, 2016).
text.formatted: In an era where digital media is increasingly integral to everyday life, young people are at the forefront of both the promises and the perils of rapidly evolving technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Livingstone, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The online environment offers opportunities, such as socializing, learning, entertainment, and identity development (Granic et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2024; Stoilova et al., 2021), but also risks, like cyberbullying, harmful content, algorithmic bias, unwanted contact or screen addiction (Livingstone & Smith, 2014; Montag et al., 2024; Sotnikova et al., 2021b; Timmis et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The online environment offers opportunities, such as socializing, learning, entertainment, and identity development <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Granic et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soh et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Stoilova et al., 2021)</ref>, but also risks, like cyberbullying, harmful content, algorithmic bias, unwanted contact or screen addiction <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Livingstone & Smith, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Montag et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sotnikova et al., 2021b;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Timmis et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In response to perceived risks and opportunities, researchers and practitioners have developed digital media interventions.

In this study, digital media interventions are defined as planned, structured programs designed to equip young people with the knowledge, skills, and habits they need to navigate digital life responsibly (Anonymous, 2026).
text.formatted: In this study, digital media interventions are defined as planned, structured programs designed to equip young people with the knowledge, skills, and habits they need to navigate digital life responsibly <ref type="bibr">(Anonymous, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions might occur with or without caregiver and teacher support, sharing a common goal: to foster sustained and responsible digital engagement.

A scoping review of existing media interventions has argued that the current field conceptualizes young people's online experiences primarily as binary terms, categorizing interventions as either risk-reducing or opportunity-enhancing (Anonymous, 2026).
text.formatted: A scoping review of existing media interventions has argued that the current field conceptualizes young people's online experiences primarily as binary terms, categorizing interventions as either risk-reducing or opportunity-enhancing <ref type="bibr">(Anonymous, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This binary framing, however, says little about the more specific dimensions of digital experience that interventions target, leaving open which aspects of young people's digital lives are well covered and which are neglected.

A likely source of this binary framing is the way youth are conceptually positioned in digital media discourse, reflecting broader tendencies to frame children as either vulnerable or empowered (Bitto-Urbanova, 2023; Stavropoulos et al., 2021; Carcelen-Garcia et al., 2023; European Institute for Gender Equality, 2019).
text.formatted: A likely source of this binary framing is the way youth are conceptually positioned in digital media discourse, reflecting broader tendencies to frame children as either vulnerable or empowered <ref type="bibr">(Bitto-Urbanova, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stavropoulos et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Carcelen-Garcia et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">European Institute for Gender Equality, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The vulnerability framing has dominated the field: research on children's digital media has historically centered risks and media effects, often at the expense of children's rights, participation, and opportunities (Livingstone, 2016; Niestadt, 2025).
text.formatted: The vulnerability framing has dominated the field: research on children's digital media has historically centered risks and media effects, often at the expense of children's rights, participation, and opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Livingstone, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Niestadt, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This historical emphasis persists in current interventions, which continue to veer towards risk reduction rather than realizing opportunities (Anonymous, 2026).
text.formatted: This historical emphasis persists in current interventions, which continue to veer towards risk reduction rather than realizing opportunities <ref type="bibr">(Anonymous, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Risk-only interventions can entrench overprotective narratives of digital childhood, while opportunity-only ones may obscure structural and interpersonal threats.

Given this tension, scholars argue that media literacy should integrate both aims -protecting young people while also enabling them to engage with media critically, creatively, and actively (Hobbs & Cappello, 2011; Hobbs, 2017).
text.formatted: Given this tension, scholars argue that media literacy should integrate both aims -protecting young people while also enabling them to engage with media critically, creatively, and actively <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hobbs & Cappello, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hobbs, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Protection and empowerment, in this view, are not opposing but complementary goals (OECD, 2025).
text.formatted: Protection and empowerment, in this view, are not opposing but complementary goals <ref type="bibr">(OECD, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To provide greater specificity, research commonly draws on the 4Cs classification of online risks (Livingstone & Stoilova, 2021) (referred to in this review as the 4C framework), which organizes children's online experiences into four dimensions: content (exposure to online information and media), contact (interactions with peers and adults online), conduct (children's own online behaviors and participation), and contract (engagement with data practices, commercial activities, and digital agreements) (Livingstone & Stoilova, 2021; Mascheroni, 2018).
text.formatted: To provide greater specificity, research commonly draws on the 4Cs classification of online risks <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Livingstone & Stoilova, 2021)</ref> (referred to in this review as the 4C framework), which organizes children's online experiences into four dimensions: content (exposure to online information and media), contact (interactions with peers and adults online), conduct (children's own online behaviors and participation), and contract (engagement with data practices, commercial activities, and digital agreements) <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Livingstone & Stoilova, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Mascheroni, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Within each of these dimensions, young people may encounter both risks and opportunities.

For example, content may expose youth to harmful or misleading information while also supporting learning; contact may involve grooming but also foster social connection; conduct may encompass harmful online behavior as well as creativity and civic participation; and contract may involve exploitative data practices alongside opportunities to develop privacy awareness and digital agency.
Although the 4C framework is widely used to classify digital risks, its application to opportunities remains underdeveloped in the intervention literature.
We therefore extend the framework to examine how interventions address both risks and opportunities across the content, contact, conduct, and contract dimensions.
This enables a more nuanced understanding of intervention design than a simple binary distinction between risk reduction and opportunity enhancement.
Based on this approach, interventions can be differentiated according to whether they address risks, opportunities, or a combination of both.
The operationalization of these categories is detailed in the Methods section.
While the 4C framework helps identify what digital media interventions target, it does not reveal how research on these intervention themes is organized or how the field has developed over time.
To address these questions, a scientometric perspective is needed.
Intervention priorities do not exist in a static environment.

New technologies and platforms constantly reshape youth's online experiences, generating emerging risks (e.g., commercialization of youth data; Rozendaal & Buijzen, 2022b and opportunities (e.g., AI-enabled personalized learning; Pataranutaporn et al., 2021), and intervention development may struggle to keep pace with these shifts, leaving gaps in both research coverage and practical implementation.
text.formatted: New technologies and platforms constantly reshape youth's online experiences, generating emerging risks (e.g., commercialization of youth data; Rozendaal & Buijzen, 2022b and opportunities (e.g., AI-enabled personalized learning; <ref type="bibr">Pataranutaporn et al., 2021)</ref>, and intervention development may struggle to keep pace with these shifts, leaving gaps in both research coverage and practical implementation.

text.text: Indeed, mapping the thematic content of interventions at a single point in time offers only a snapshot of a field that is itself a moving target; a fuller understanding of how these themes are organized, interconnected, and have evolved over time is needed.

Scientometric approaches are particularly well suited to this task because they reveal the intellectual structure of a research field, identify dominant and emerging topics, and trace changes in research emphasis over time (Chen & Song, 2019; Donthu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Scientometric approaches are particularly well suited to this task because they reveal the intellectual structure of a research field, identify dominant and emerging topics, and trace changes in research emphasis over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chen & Song, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Donthu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To trace how thematic emphasis has shifted, intervention type and 4C risk/opportunity categories are displayed separately, showing which intervention types and 4C categories became more prominent over time.
Lastly, understanding which topics are gaining or losing prominence can be complemented by examining who is producing this knowledge, and how well-connected that knowledge base is.
Digital media interventions address complex, multidimensional problems that span education, youth care, and public health (Anonymous, 2026).

Fields of this kind benefit from cross-disciplinary and cross-institutional collaboration, because integrating diverse expertise supports more comprehensive intervention design (Leydesdorff & Rafols, 2011b.
text.formatted: Fields of this kind benefit from cross-disciplinary and cross-institutional collaboration, because integrating diverse expertise supports more comprehensive intervention design <ref type="bibr">(Leydesdorff & Rafols, 2011b</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, fragmented collaboration networks, in which researchers cluster within narrow sub-specialties, can lead to siloed knowledge production and duplicated efforts, slowing the field's collective progress (Newman, 2001; Uddin et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Conversely, fragmented collaboration networks, in which researchers cluster within narrow sub-specialties, can lead to siloed knowledge production and duplicated efforts, slowing the field's collective progress <ref type="bibr">(Newman, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Uddin et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The extent to which researchers collaborate across these boundaries may shape how effectively the field addresses the full scope of young people's digital experiences identified above.

To tackle this, we examine co-authorship patterns to assess how knowledge production in this field is organized, and whether collaboration reflects the same fragmentation observed in the field's thematic focus.
Citation patterns and bibliographic coupling further reveal how sub-communities within the field relate to one another intellectually, beyond who co-authors with whom.

The three elements mentioned above (i.e. the thematic focus of digital media interventions, the evolution of intervention priorities over time, and the structure of research collaboration and knowledge production) can inform decision-making among researchers, policymakers, educators, and funding agencies, supporting continued development of digital media interventions and better outcomes for youth.
Specifically, we address the following questions:
RQ1: How are digital media interventions distributed across the 4C risk and opportunity dimensions (or categories), and to what extent do they address these in interconnected or combined ways?
RQ2: How have the risks and opportunities targeted by digital media interventions changed over time?
RQ3: What collaboration networks, citation patterns, and bibliographic coupling clusters characterize the field, and what do these reveal about its structural and disciplinary evolution?

Together, these methods constitute a hybrid review that combines scoping elements with the main scientometric approach to examine the content, evolution, and structure of research on digital media interventions.
This scientometric review builds on a dataset of empirical studies on digital media interventions among youth that was originally compiled for a previous scoping review (Anonymous, 2026).
text.formatted: This scientometric review builds on a dataset of empirical studies on digital media interventions among youth that was originally compiled for a previous scoping review <ref type="bibr">(Anonymous, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: That review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and was reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines.

While the scoping review mapped the content of digital media interventions, the present study uses the same dataset to examine publication patterns, research networks, and thematic clusters through scientometric analyses using VOSviewer (Van Eck & Waltman, 2010).
text.formatted: While the scoping review mapped the content of digital media interventions, the present study uses the same dataset to examine publication patterns, research networks, and thematic clusters through scientometric analyses using VOSviewer <ref type="bibr">(Van Eck & Waltman, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The search strategy targeted three core concepts: youth, digital media interventions, and effectiveness evaluation.

This search was executed across four databases (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, and the Psychology & Behavioral Sciences Collection) without restrictions on publication date or full-text language.
text.formatted: This search was executed across four databases (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, and the Psychology & Behavioral Sciences Collection) without restrictions on publication date or full-text language.

text.text: Studies were included if they: (1) involved young people aged less than or equal to 23 years, or their caregivers/educators, which was chosen to reflect the educational and legal provisions that extend into young adulthood; (2) examined planned digital media interventions aimed at developing digital skills, literacy, safe/healthy online behaviors, or related competencies; (3) used experimental or quasi-experimental group designs; and (4) were published as peer-reviewed articles with at least an English-language abstract.
Studies focusing solely on nondigital media or belonging to the grey literature were excluded.
In addition to database searches, citation tracking and targeted searches identified additional studies.
After deduplication, screening, and full-text assessment, the final dataset comprised 120 studies.
The 120 empirical studies described 131 distinct evaluations of digital media interventions.
Complete search strings, screening procedures, and the PRISMA flow diagram are reported in Anonymous (2026).

To supplement the variables collected in the original scoping review, we identified the specific risks and opportunities addressed and categorized them under the 4C framework (i.e. content, contact, conduct, and contract) (see Table 1).
text.formatted: To supplement the variables collected in the original scoping review, we identified the specific risks and opportunities addressed and categorized them under the 4C framework (i.e. content, contact, conduct, and contract) (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Although the 4C framework can be combined with additional dimensions, such as risk typologies (e.g., aggressive, sexual, or values-related risks), preliminary coding revealed limited variation across these dimensions.
Therefore, we focused exclusively on the 4C typology.

Based on this coding, interventions were classified into four overarching categories: (1) risk-only, addressing only risks; (2) opportunity-only, addressing only opportunities; (3) dual-linked, addressing both risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension; and (4) dualmixed, addressing risks and opportunities across different 4C dimensions.

For example, an intervention that teaches adolescents to critically evaluate online advertising (contract risk) while also building digital literacy skills (content opportunity) would be coded as dual-mixed.
A program addressing social media interactions as a harmful conduct risk and as a conduct opportunity to build creative participation would be coded as dual-linked.
Two researchers independently coded the first 50 studies, showing substantial agreement (PABAK = 0.68-0.88; Byrt et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Two researchers independently coded the first 50 studies, showing substantial agreement (PABAK = 0.68-0.88; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Byrt et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: The remaining 70 studies were coded by one researcher.

For RQ1, we quantified how often each 4C dimension, and each intervention type, appeared across the included studies, allowing us to map which risks and opportunities are most frequently targeted and how they co-occur within interventions.

For RQ2, we tracked how these same intervention types and 4C categories shifted in frequency over the study period, visualizing publication trends to identify which types and categories became more or less prominent over time, as well as the emergence of new thematic emphases.

For RQ3, we used VOSviewer (Van Eck & Waltman, 2010) to examine co-authorship networks, citation relations, and bibliographic coupling, identifying influential publications, and collaborative communities.
text.formatted: For RQ3, we used VOSviewer <ref type="bibr">(Van Eck & Waltman, 2010)</ref> to examine co-authorship networks, citation relations, and bibliographic coupling, identifying influential publications, and collaborative communities.

text.text: RQ3 analyses revealed how scholarly impact was distributed, which researchers or institutions functioned as central nodes in the field, and how different streams of intervention research were interconnected.

Of the 120 included studies, 27 were retained in the citation network analysis, whereas 93 studies had no direct citation links with other publications within the dataset and were therefore excluded from the visualized citation network.
We used association strength normalization for all network visualizations.
An additional keyword co-occurrence analysis was conducted with VOSviewer on author keywords with a minimum of 2 occurrences per keyword.
Clustering used a resolution of 1.00.
Fair and transparent data practices, privacy protection, and safe digital environments Figure 1 illustrates the growth of digital media intervention literature over time.
text.formatted: Fair and transparent data practices, privacy protection, and safe digital environments Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> illustrates the growth of digital media intervention literature over time.

text.text: Publication activity was limited in the earliest years covered by the corpus.
The first evaluation appeared in 2006, and no more than three studies were published in any year before 2014.
Together, these years account for just 10 of the 120 studies (8.3%).
From 2014 onward, output became more consistent, with 5-13 evaluations published annually through 2021.
Growth then accelerated sharply.
Half of all evaluations in the corpus (50.8%) were published between 2020 and 2024, and 38.3% appeared during 2022-2024 alone.
Annual output peaked in 2023 with 19 studies (15.8% of the corpus), and the median publication year was 2020.
Although the included evaluations originated from a broad range of countries, Figure 2 demonstrates that research activity was unevenly distributed across geographic regions.
text.formatted: Although the included evaluations originated from a broad range of countries, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> demonstrates that research activity was unevenly distributed across geographic regions.

text.text: A relatively small number of countries accounted for a substantial share of the evidence base, particularly the United States and several Western European countries.
In contrast, relatively few evaluations were conducted in many parts of Africa, South America, and the Middle East.

Thus, while the literature has achieved broad international reach, the available evidence remains geographically concentrated, raising questions about how well existing intervention findings generalize across different cultural, educational, and technological contexts.
The keyword co-occurrence analysis (Figure 3) indicates that the literature is organized around several distinct thematic clusters rather than a single, uniform intervention focus.
text.formatted: The keyword co-occurrence analysis (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>) indicates that the literature is organized around several distinct thematic clusters rather than a single, uniform intervention focus.

text.text: Three prominent clusters center on related but distinguishable forms of literacy: media literacy, digital literacy, and information literacy.
This suggests that a substantial portion of the field approaches digital media intervention through educational and competency-building frameworks.

Other clusters reflect more risk-focused intervention targets, particularly cyberbullying and related concepts such as empathy and prevention, as well as a smaller cluster focused on screen time, mobile phone use, and internet use.
These patterns suggest that the literacy-oriented approaches form a prominent component in interventions alongside interventions targeting specific digital risks and behaviors.
Across the 120 studies, 39.2% (n = 47) used dual-linked interventions, which address risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension.
For example, Belova and Krause ( 2023   combine risks and opportunities from different 4C dimensions.
text.formatted: For example, Belova and Krause ( <ref type="formula">2023</ref>   combine risks and opportunities from different 4C dimensions.

text.text: Overall, 97.5% of studies operated within a single 4C dimension, and cross-dimensional approaches remain rare.
Figure 4 descriptively summarizes the distribution of the 4C dimensions across intervention types.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref> descriptively summarizes the distribution of the 4C dimensions across intervention types.

text.text: Among risk-only interventions, conduct-related risks, including cyberbullying and other harmful online behaviors, appeared frequently.
Opportunity-only interventions were commonly associated with content-related opportunities, including digital literacy, critical information evaluation, and educational media use.
Dual-mixed interventions most often involved combinations of conduct-related risks and content-related opportunities, while contact and contract dimensions appeared less frequently.
Dual linked interventions included interventions across several 4C dimensions.

Given the small number of interventions in some categories, these patterns should be interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence of statistically reliable differences between intervention types.
4.2 Risks and Opportunity Distribution over Time (RQ2) Figure 5 shows changes in the distribution of intervention types over time.
In the earlier years of the field, risk-only interventions were relatively prominent, although dual-linked approaches were also present.
From the mid-2010s onward, opportunity-only and dual-linked interventions became increasingly common, indicating a broadening of the types of interventions represented in the field.

In the most recent years, dual-linked interventions showed the strongest increase and were the most frequently represented intervention type, while dual-mixed interventions remained comparatively uncommon.
Overall, the figure suggests increasing representation of interventions that address both risks and opportunities, alongside continued use of single-focus approaches.
Figure 6 shows a strong concentration of studies in the conduct and content dimensions.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">6</ref> shows a strong concentration of studies in the conduct and content dimensions.

text.text: Conduct is the most prominent category, while content follows a similar upward trend.
In contrast, contact appeared far less frequently, and contract was the least represented across the entire period.

From 2022 to 2024, conduct and content together accounted for over 80% of all coded instances, underscoring the field's growing emphasis on behavioral and content-related aspects of youth's digital media use, while contact and especially contract remained comparatively untapped.

4.3 Impact and Collaboration in Digital Media Interventions (RQ3) According to Scopus, retrieved on 04/03/2026, the included studies were cited by others with an average of 64.82 times (min = 0; max = 386; SD = 77.36).
The co-authorship analysis reveals a fragmented collaboration structure, characterized by several distinct author clusters rather than a single integrated network (Figure 7).
text.formatted: The co-authorship analysis reveals a fragmented collaboration structure, characterized by several distinct author clusters rather than a single integrated network (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">7</ref>).

text.text: These clusters represented research "islands," consistent with the specialization of topics within the field.

For example, one cluster centered around authors such as Hudders whose work focuses on the influence of marketing, whereas another cluster was formed by Del Rey and colleagues, who consistently published on cyberbullying interventions.
Such groupings suggest that researchers mainly collaborate within their own thematic niche, rather than across different areas of digital media intervention research.

Unlike the co-authorship analysis in Figure 7, which reveals the extent to which researchers collaborate in this field, the citation-document analysis in Figure 8 shows how publications are linked through citations and how influence flows between them.

text.text: This analysis identified a few highly central studies, with works such as Williford et al. (2013) and Cross et al. ( 2015) functioning as key citation hubs.

Notably, 93 publications had no direct citation links with other publications within the dataset, suggesting a considerable degree of fragmentation within the literature.
This pattern mirrored the topical fragmentation of the field: authors collaborated within narrow subdomains, and their work was also most frequently cited within those same specialized clusters.

text.text: Within this structure, Sarah McGrew, Mariska Kleemans, and Martin Valcke appeared as relatively central figures, reflecting their use of widely cited foundational literature.

These publications primarily addressed topics such as digital literacy, media literacy, online information evaluation, cyberbullying, and digital citizenship, indicating that these themes were among the more commonly shared reference points within the field.
Overall, the results suggest that, despite thematic fragmentation, some overlap exists in the literature on which studies draw.

This scientometric review with scoping elements examined how digital media interventions for youth are distributed across risk-and opportunity-focused approaches, how these emphases have evolved over time, and how the research field is structurally organized in terms of collaboration and knowledge production.

The key scoping finding is that, although most interventions still treat risks and opportunities separately, integration within the same 4C dimension has become more common: dual-linked interventions form the largest single category and are now the most frequent type.
Integration across different 4C dimensions, in contrast, remains rare.

Regarding intervention objectives, most interventions focus on individual behavior and content-related outcomes (i.e., conduct and content), while social interaction and data privacy concerns (i.e., contact and contract) receive comparatively limited attention.
Bibliographic coupling showed that, despite the presence of distinct thematic clusters, some studies shared a common body of foundational literature.
Studies on digital literacy, media literacy, cyberbullying, online information evaluation, and digital citizenship shared several core references and formed areas of intellectual overlap.

Taken together, the scoping and scientometric findings suggest that the field has developed considerable expertise within specific intervention dimensions, but that integration across dimensions remains limited.

While such specialization may be valuable for generating depth and advancing knowledge for particular topics, it may also mean that insights from areas such as digital literacy, cyberbullying, digital citizenship, and online information evaluation are not always combined within the same intervention approach.
This interpretation is consistent with our finding that interventions rarely integrate risks and opportunities across different 4C dimensions.
The distribution of intervention types suggests that the field is moving from a protection-focused perspective toward a more integrated understanding of youth's digital media use.
However, this integration remains bounded: it operates within a single dimension rather than across the full complexity of youth's digital lives.
Dual-mixed designs, which combine risk mitigation and opportunity enhancement across different 4C dimensions, remain marginal.
This gap is conceptually significant.

Since youth's digital experiences do not naturally partition into risks or opportunities, nor unfold within a single dimension at a time, a single interaction or platform can simultaneously afford learning, social connection, exposure to harmful content, and data exploitation.

This suggests that intervention design should be informed by an awareness of these interdependencies, so that even narrowly scoped interventions account for how the dimension they target relates to others, rather than treating risks and opportunities as if they operate in isolation.
Additionally, the temporal data offer some grounds for cautious optimism.
Risk-only approaches were most common in early intervention research, consistent with a protective paradigm in which children were primarily positioned as vulnerable subjects requiring safeguarding.
From the mid-2010s onward, opportunity-oriented and dual-linked designs became increasingly prevalent, signaling a gradual reconceptualization of young people as active digital participants.

This trajectory, from protection toward empowerment and, tentatively, toward integration, mirrors broader shifts in the theoretical framing of childhood and digital media (Livingstone et al., 2017; Stavropoulos et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This trajectory, from protection toward empowerment and, tentatively, toward integration, mirrors broader shifts in the theoretical framing of childhood and digital media <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Livingstone et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stavropoulos et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Yet this transition remains incomplete and uneven.
The field has begun to move beyond purely protective models but has not yet arrived at holistic frameworks of digital wellbeing that reflect the interconnected nature of youth's online experiences.

A more detailed finding concerns the imbalance between the 4C dimensions, with relatively more attention being paid to content and conduct risks and opportunities, and less attention to contact and contract.

The dominance of conduct-focused interventions, particularly anti-cyberbullying programs, and content-focused approaches centered on media and digital literacy reflect historical patterns, yet their prominence may partly be an artifact of legacy paradigms rather than a deliberate response to current digital realities.
Less attention has been paid to contact-based risks and opportunities, encompassing peer dynamics, social networking, and interactions with unknown adults.
Those experiences remain underrepresented despite their centrality in young people's everyday digital lives (Livingstone & Smith, 2014; Cernikova et al., 2016).

text.text: The contract dimension being least represented is perhaps the most striking finding in this regard.

As youth's digital environments are increasingly shaped by data collection practices, algorithmic personalization, and platform-driven commercialization, the absence of interventions addressing these structural forces suggests that the field has yet to fully grapple with the datafication of childhood (Rozendaal & Buijzen, 2022b.
text.formatted: As youth's digital environments are increasingly shaped by data collection practices, algorithmic personalization, and platform-driven commercialization, the absence of interventions addressing these structural forces suggests that the field has yet to fully grapple with the datafication of childhood (Rozendaal & Buijzen, 2022b.

text.text: Emerging risks such as microtargeting, dark-pattern design, and the commercial exploitation of youth data fall almost entirely outside the current intervention landscape.

Taken together, these patterns suggest that the field is well-resourced in dimensions where risks are visible and pedagogically tractable but poorly equipped for the platform-governance and data-rights challenges that define contemporary digital childhood.
Across all three bibliometric analyses, a consistent picture emerges: collaboration, citation, and shared intellectual foundations each map onto the same thematic boundaries.
Researchers tended to publish, collaborate, and cite work within established domains such as cyberbullying, digital literacy, news literacy, online information evaluation, and digital citizenship.
At the same time, the bibliographic coupling analysis indicated that these domains were not entirely disconnected.

Publications occupying relatively central positions in the network, including work by McGrew, Kleemans, and Valcke, drew on core literature related to digital literacy, media literacy, online information evaluation, cyberbullying, and digital citizenship, creating areas of overlap across otherwise distinct research strands.
These findings suggest that the field combines specialization with a limited set of shared intellectual foundations.
Such specialization is not necessarily problematic and may support the development of theoretical depth and domain-specific expertise.

However, when considered alongside the scoping findings, it appears that insights from these different domains are only occasionally translated into intervention approaches that integrate multiple risks and opportunities.

For example, research on cyberbullying, digital literacy, online information evaluation, and privacy-related issues develops within separate intervention traditions, despite drawing on some of the same foundational ideas.

The relatively small number of dual-mixed interventions identified in this review may therefore reflect the continued organization of the field around specific thematic domains, even where common conceptual foundations exist.
The findings carry distinct implications for three groups of stakeholders: intervention designers and practitioners, funders and policymakers, and researchers.
For researchers, on collaboration.
First, our network analysis shows that intervention researchers mostly stay within their own topic area.
They collaborate with, cite, and build on the work of others in the same niche (e.g., cyberbullying or digital literacy), but rarely cross into other author clusters.

Professional organizations could actively create opportunities for different teams to work together, for example by funding joint projects that pair a cyberbullying researcher with a privacy researcher.
Second, our bibliographic coupling results show that some studies from different clusters already draw on shared foundational sources, even without directly citing or collaborating with each other.
These existing points of overlap could be used as natural starting points for collaborative reviews, workshops, or shared research frameworks.
For intervention designers and practitioners.
The 4C imbalance reveals that contact and contract dimensions present knowledge gaps for intervention.

Concretely, this means developing curricula that address peer-network navigation and interactions with unknown adults (contact) with the same rigor currently applied to anti-cyberbullying programming and developing data-literacy and algorithmic-awareness modules (contract) that go beyond generic "privacy settings" tutorials to address microtargeting, dark-pattern recognition, and commercial data exploitation specifically.
Because dual-mixed designs remain marginal, practitioners should consider utilizing crossdimensional pairing in intervention design.

For example, a module combining contract-based data literacy content with identity-dimension social-connection content could test whether teaching youth to recognize how platforms monetize their self-expression changes how they engage in identity related risk-taking.
This requires moving intervention development towards including content that specifies how a single online interaction can simultaneously produce risk exposure and developmental opportunity.
For funders and policymakers.

Funders should prioritize the allocation of resources towards the development of contract dimension interventions (data rights, algorithmic transparency, commercial exploitation) and dual-mixed designs that cut across different topic dimensions.

Policymakers aiming to improve youth's online safety should recognize that the current evidence base is heavily concentrated on cyberbullying and digital literacy, while datafication-related issues receive considerably less attention.

As a result, current intervention evidence may provide only a partial picture of the challenges youth face online, and policy decisions should not be guided solely by the areas that have received the most research attention.

Taken together, closing the 4C gap requires funders, journals, and professional networks to actively engineer collaboration and gather of resources, which the scientometric analysis shows is not occurring on its own.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, only the first 50 studies were independently coded by two researchers (PABAK = 0.68-0.88; Byrt et al., 1993).

text.text: The remaining 70 were coded by a single researcher using the resulting codebook.
Second, the dualmixed category contains only three interventions, so findings for this category are descriptive and should not be generalized.
Finally, the corpus is limited to experimental and quasi-experimental evaluations.
Our conclusions therefore describe this particular segment rather than the full field of digital media intervention research.
This study set out to understand not only what research on digital media interventions for youth addresses, but how the research field studying these interventions is organized.
The value of the hybrid approach lies precisely in showing that these two questions are connected.

A field that develops in disconnected thematic clusters is, perhaps unsurprisingly, one that produces disconnected interventions; the content gaps identified in the scoping review and the structural fragmentation identified in the scientometric analysis are best understood as two expressions of the same underlying dynamic rather than separate problems.

Addressing this will require more than isolated calls for "more integrated interventions", as it points to a need for the field's incentive structures, funding bodies, and publication venues to actively reward cross-cluster collaboration and cross-dimensional design, rather than leaving integration to individual researchers working within already-existing niches.

As digital platforms continue to reshape the risks and opportunities young people encounter, closing this gap between fragmented knowledge production and the integrated nature of youth's digital lives will be essential for intervention research to remain relevant to the environments it seeks to address.
